canberra.title: New ice sports facility proposal can now be better located and less costly, says development partner
canberra.snippet: The dumping of the Tuggeranong option for an ice sports facility can clear the way for a less expensive and more viable development, one ...
canberra.content:
The success of the Canberra Brave at AIS Arena means a new ice sports facility proposal can be more modest. Photo: Verity Griffin.

The dumping of the Tuggeranong option for an ice sports facility can clear the way for a less expensive and more viable development, one of the proponents has said.

Cruachan Investments director Stephen Campbell, who also doubles as the owner of the ice hockey franchise the Canberra Brave, is putting a positive spin on the ACT Government’s decision, saying it was right to see the Tuggeranong proposal as not offering value for money and as too risky.

He said he and development partner Pelligra had doubts about the Greenway site from the start but tried to make it work, only for costs to blow out as the problems with the sloping, treed site became better known.

But Mr Campbell, whose interests with the Brave diverge from the other ice sports participants, has been pushing for a more central location for some time.

He said two unnamed better locations were already in the frame.

“We have two sites that we have been concurrently investigating, and we’ll put a future proposal to government which will involve one or both of those sites that will be a far more modest, and we think economically achievable project,” Mr Campbell said.

The Brave’s successful move to the AIS Arena this winter confirmed to him that any new ice sports facility would not require as much spectator space, with the long-term vision for elite ice hockey now to find a home at the proposed Convention and Entertainment Centre in Civic.

While the Brave now has a home venue to play in, it will still require ice to train on, ideally from February before the start of the season, which runs from late April to the end of August.

At present, it can only train when the ice goes in at the AIS Arena, because the Brave do not have access to the Phillip Ice Skating Centre, although it is seeking time there next year.

Mr Campbell said any new facility would not need seating for 3000 as envisaged at Tuggeranong but only about 500.

It would still require two sheets to cater for sporting and recreational use, but the more modest development would bring the cost down to a more manageable level that government could entertain.

Cruachan Investments director and Canberra Brave owner Stephen Campbell says a better outcome is now possible. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

Officials broke the expected news to him on Monday, and Mr Campbell came away encouraged that the government still recognised the need for an ice sports facility.

Mr Campbell said this would still require a partnership with a private developer.

He said the growing popularity of the Brave and interest in ice sports generally justified committing taxpayer dollars to a new proposal.

“If you look at aggregate attendance at sporting events, Canberra Brave is second only to the Raiders in the ACT, so there is huge support. That success has also translated into growth at the grassroots level.

“We’ve seen junior and women’s ice hockey in particular grow four to fivefold. It’s no longer a fringe sport, so there is a need for infrastructure.”

While the more traditional sports had greater numbers, without the facilities, there could be no participation.

The picture becomes murky when considering just who will be talking to the government, given the ACT Ice Sports Federation spokesperson Sandi Logan expressed doubts about Cruachan’s ability to deliver two ice rinks in Adelaide.

Mr Campbell said community opposition to the felling of two trees scuppered one proposal, while the other was likely to go ahead.

“We will put a separate proposal for a solution for ice sports, and I’m sure the Ice Sports Federation will have discussions with the government and the government may choose to have separate discussions with other bodies, but you know I’m optimistic,” he said.

In the meantime, he expected the Phillip rink to keep operating if it is well maintained.

“There’s a good group [Geocon] who are operating it, and I expect that it’ll be there to service the Canberra community until such time as there is a new facility,” Mr Campbell said.

Geocon was contacted for comment.

canberra.title: ‘Stop the tax’: Canberra looked up and asked, which one?
canberra.snippet: Canberra is used to political messages. They are usually delivered in Parliament, at a press conference or, when things get particularly ...
canberra.content:
‘STOP THE TAX’ appeared in the skies above Canberra on Tuesday (8 September). Photo: Syed Sabihur Rahman.

Canberra is used to political messages. They are usually delivered in Parliament, at a press conference or, when things get particularly heated, on the lawns outside. On Tuesday morning (8 September), someone decided the sky would do.

The man behind it was Sydney mortgage broker and entrepreneur Joseph Daoud, who had arrived in Canberra for a charity tennis match with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at The Lodge – and decided to bring his campaign against the Federal Government’s capital gains tax changes with him.

At about 11 am, a plane began writing the message above the capital in enormous white letters.

There was just one problem.

Which tax?

Daoud had deliberately commissioned “STOP THE TAX” over Canberra, while a second aerial campaign over Brisbane carried the fuller message “STOP TAXING AMBITION”.

Daoud, founder of It’s Simple Finance, is behind the Stop the Ambition Tax campaign and argues the government’s capital gains tax and negative gearing changes will hurt small business owners, investors and people trying to build wealth.

And the timing of Tuesday’s airborne protest was no coincidence.

In August, Daoud paid $16,500 at a charity auction to secure a tennis match with Mr Albanese at The Lodge.

“Today I play the Prime Minister at tennis. Before he looks across the net at me, I want him to look up. Stop the Ambition Tax,” he told Region in a statement.

The idea for taking the campaign quite literally to another level apparently came over dinner at his mother’s house.

“I was sitting at Mum’s table the other night eating her famous chicken shawarma, thinking about how we make sure this match is about more than a game of tennis,” Daoud said.

“The only way left was up. So we went up.”

But while Daoud knew exactly which tax he was talking about, plenty of people looking skywards in Canberra did not.

The skywriter offered no footnotes, explanatory memorandum or QR code. And in a city that knows its taxes, Canberra did what Canberra does best – began debating the details.

The guesses came quickly on social media: beer tax, cigarette tax, airport tax, aviation fuel tax, even a “thumb tax”.

Some thought the missing word was simply “all”.

One commenter guessed it was about tobacco tax, but joked that adding “on tobacco” would probably have meant the plane “would be over Yass before it finished”.

Another suspected fuel tax, joking that perhaps the pilot “might’ve run out so he couldn’t finish it”.

Others suggested “smoke tax”, “sky writing smoke tax” and, inevitably, “chemtrail”.

For anyone wondering what it costs to turn Canberra’s sky into a billboard, it isn’t exactly loose change.

Online estimates from Australian operators put traditional skywriting at about $6000 and upwards, depending on the location and requirements of the flight. Skywriting Australia, for example, advertises traditional skywriting from $5990.

How much Daoud paid for Tuesday’s message has not been disclosed.

The government’s tax changes passed Parliament in June. They scrap the 50 per cent CGT discount, introduce cost-base indexation and a 30 per cent minimum tax rate. Negative gearing will also be restricted to new builds, while existing arrangements will be grandfathered for landlords already benefiting from the system.

The government argues the changes will create a fairer tax system and “level the playing field” for workers and first-home buyers. Daoud disagrees, arguing they will instead reduce housing turnover and investment.

He brought three Australians to Canberra to put their concerns directly to the Prime Minister and said the tennis match was ultimately a vehicle to get their message heard.

“Before I won this match at auction, I had never picked up a tennis racquet in my life. Now I’m on the court four or five times a week, and I’ve fallen in love with the game,” he said.

“But I’m not coming to Canberra for the tennis. I’m coming to stand up for everyday Australians who’ve had their ambition taxed, and I’m not going to waste the chance.”

Whether the message changed anyone’s mind about tax remains to be seen.

But for a few hours on Tuesday, it achieved something remarkable: it got Canberra talking about tax even when nobody had called a press conference.

canberra.title: Registered child sex offender jailed for almost seven years over more sickening offences
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to child abuse. Already being convicted for horrific crimes did not stop a man from collecting over ...
canberra.content:
The Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation made a referral to ACT Policing, which ultimately resulted in the arrest of Arryn John Morris. Photo: Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation Facebook.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to child abuse.

Already being convicted for horrific crimes did not stop a man from collecting over 1700 files related to the abuse of children, as well as directly offending against 30 children he spoke to over the internet.

Last week, the ACT Supreme Court sentenced 48-year-old Aaryn John Morris to a total of six years and 11 months’ jail with a non-parole period of two years and 10 months.

Justice Andrew Muller, in his recently published decision, said Morris had been a registered child sex offender for 20 years.

In 2006, he was convicted of two counts of committing an act of indecency on a person under 10 and one count of possessing child pornography of a person under 16.

Then in August 2024, ACT Policing heard that child abuse material had been transmitted by someone in Canberra using Morris’s email address.

Police searched his accounts and devices in June 2025 and discovered a sickening amount of such material.

There were 10 videos and 288 images on his mobile phone, 14 videos and 223 images on his iPad, and 1246 files on an online storage account.

In addition, police found horrific material in his online chat accounts.

The child abuse material showed assaults on children aged under 10. One video lasted for an hour and a half.

Morris had also directly offended against children. He posed as a child to gain access to child abuse material, while he also exposed himself to 30 different children online.

“It is a matter of significance that real children were involved in the offending, notwithstanding their identities are not known,” Justice Muller said.

“The long-term psychological impacts of childhood sexual abuse are very well recognised.”

As a registered child sex offender, Morris was required to report personal details like his email addresses, internet usernames, instant messaging usernames and chat room usernames.

“Mr Morris failed to report the details of the accounts under consideration for the subject offending,” Justice Muller said.

He said it appeared Morris’s motivation for his crimes was for his own sexual gratification and to “trade” images online with like-minded individuals.

Morris suffered an acquired brain injury due to illness when he was a child, and his cognitive functioning has been consistently assessed as significantly impaired.

He was employed in bar work and at a liquor store for about three years before his arrest for the current offending.

A psychologist thought he was not a predatory paedophile in the ordinary sense, but rather a cognitively impaired and developmentally immature man with poor cortical inhibition, immature sexual drives, and limited capacity to understand or manage those impulses.

Justice Muller said a pre-sentence report found Morris displayed limited insight into the circumstances and motivations underpinning his offending.

“Whilst describing his behaviour as ‘pretty bad’, he was unable to articulate the aspect of his behaviour that was wrong or why the behaviour was wrong,” he said.

As Morris’s non-parole period was backdated to account for time served, he will be eligible for release from April 2028.

He pleaded guilty to seven charges, including possessing child abuse material using a carriage service, failing to report as a registered person, using a carriage service for sexual activity with a person under 16 and transmitting indecent communication to a person under 16.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

You can also submit an online report about a historical sexual assault allegation for incidents that occurred more than six months ago.

canberra.title: Algorithm opt-out legislaltion released for consultation
canberra.snippet: New laws will give Australians control over their social media algorithms and put the onus on digital service providers to ensure a safe ...
canberra.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says the Digital Duty of Care legislation is about giving people control over what they see. Photo: Region.

New laws will give Australians control over their social media algorithms and put the onus on digital service providers to ensure a safe online environment for the users of their platforms.

Draft legislation for Labour’s much-anticipated Digital Duty of Care rules was released on Tuesday (8 September) for targeted consultation, but the Federal Government wants changes enshrined in law as soon as possible.

Changes will include the new ‘My Feed, My Way’ initiative, which will require social media platforms to send notifications to new and existing users, offering them an opt-out choice regarding their default feeds.

Users can choose to opt in to having personalised content recommended by the algorithm, or opt out of personally recommended content, allowing them to see the friends and creators they choose to follow.

Online games, apps and AI chatbots will be required to protect under-18s from design features that have negative behavioural impacts, such as addictive features or those that can affect a young person’s self-esteem.

These include content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; hostile ideas about women and gender equality; pornography; glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; or causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.

But the Prime Minister strongly refuted any suggestion the bill could amount to political censorship.

“It’s not about censorship. It’s about giving people control themselves over what they see,” Mr Albanese said.

“We can emphatically rule that out. This is about basic safety standards online for online services and about the onus being on big tech to identify risks on their platform and to mitigate against those risks.”

Together with Communications Minister Anika Wells and several high-profile advocates for imposing more controls on social media, the Prime Minister detailed the legislation at a courtyard media conference at Parliament House.

The PM followed up with an explanation during Question Time, saying the government had listened to Australians who are saying “enough is enough”.

He said the government was open to discussing the bill and is seeking feedback from digital platforms, industry bodies, civil society organisations and advocates on the draft laws.

The intent is to introduce the legislation to parliament in October, and Labor is hoping for broad consensus.

“This is not about giving government control; it is about giving people control,” Mr Albanese said.

“Today we are releasing the government’s approach to give Australians choice over their online experience, ‘My Feed, My Way’.

“Australia is leading the world with our social media age ban and online safety approach.

“This work has been led by parents and advocates, and we have backed them. We will continue to do so.”

The draft laws provide eSafety with the power to issue removal notices for ‘nudify’ apps or websites, and to streamline the child cyber-bullying and adult cyber abuse schemes to enable eSafety to deal more quickly with this harmful material.

Nudify apps use AI-generated software to turn photographs of people wearing clothing into naked or pornographic images.

Digital platforms will be required to document the measures taken to address identified risks of harm to Australian users and ensure these measures remain effective over time.

Ms Wells said the government was taking the next step following its world-leading social media age ban for under 16s.

She said the opt-out provision, rather than a stronger opt-in model the Greens and others have suggested, was “through the middle” and allows people to choose what type of feeds they want to receive.

“Just as we have basic safety standards for cars, toys or food, the duty of care applies basic standards for the online products we use every day,” the minister said.

“When it comes to social media, Australians over the age of 16 will be able to opt in or opt out of the algorithm easily. The duty of care will require platforms to give users over 16 a choice about which feed they see when they open the app – and to respect that choice.

“The digital duty of care will ensure online service providers – including some of the most powerful companies in the world – step up and do more to keep Australians safe from harm on their platforms.”

The Coalition isn’t jumping onboard straight away.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has already raised concerns about government overreach, and Nationals Leader Matt Canavan took to social media immediately after the announcement, saying the government should not be trusted on the issue.

Senator Canavan said Labor’s goal was to censor people.

“Rather than trying to rig the algorithm, the government should focus on fixing the problems of too high prices, too much tax and too much migration,” he said.

The Democracy Counts alliance, however, welcomed the draft legislation.

“Fifteen years ago there was a feeling that social media was going to save democracy, but what we’ve seen since is extreme polarisation and a breakdown of trust,” campaign director Tom Mooney said.

“A healthy democracy requires people to start with a shared set of facts, and to be aware of the different experiences and opinions of others.

“But the algorithms are locking us in echo chambers, and that’s a major contributor to declining trust in our democracy and democratic institutions.”

australia.title: Mother flagged faulty smoke alarms before house fire that killed father and five children, court hears
australia.snippet: Pre-inquest conference into Queensland deaths hears witnesses did not hear any smoke alarms during 2023 fire Get our breaking news email ...
australia.content:
A landlord was repeatedly warned about improperly installed smoke alarms before a house fire that killed a father and five children in Queensland in 2023, a coroner has heard.

Deputy state coroner Donald MacKenzie held a pre-inquest conference into the Russell Island deaths on Tuesday.

No witness recalls hearing the sound of an alarm during the blaze, it heard.

The owner was fined $774 for improper installation in 2024, the maximum possible penalty under Queensland law. A conviction was not recorded.

The fire in the two-storey wooden Queenslander broke out on 6 August 2023. The house had been moved to the island and then renovated in 2013 before being rented privately.

Five children – two brothers aged four and others aged three, 10 and 11 – died in the blaze. Their father, 34, died after running into the fire to rescue them. None can be identified for legal reasons.

The children’s mother and father had fallen asleep in a converted “chill out” area underneath the house.

The father awoke to see thick black smoke and immediately raced upstairs, where the children were sleeping.

His partner also tried to get into the house, but was forced back by the fire. Another adult woman leapt off a balcony to safety and survived.

The Queensland fire department does not have a station on Russell Island, and vehicles must be ferried over in an emergency, a process that takes about 45-60 minutes, the court heard.

As a result, it was a paramedic who first arrived at the scene, arriving within minutes at about 6.26am.

“He recalls that the fire’s heat was so intense that he could feel it through his vehicle window, and could see the flames coming from the roof and smoke in a mushroom formation,” counsel assisting Corinne Leach told the court.

“[The children’s mother] was kneeling on the ground in complete distress with [the other woman] beside her. He asked if anyone else was inside, to which [the mother} replied: her five children, and lost all ability to communicate.”

The paramedic also tried to get into the building but was halted by the intense blaze. He instead focused on evacuating neighbouring homes. Rural firefighters arrived at 6.35am.

The court heard the home had poor wiring, an exposed electrical box and faulty power points, known to short out. It also had an extension cord running from a poorly operating power point in a child’s bedroom, from a double adapter, to the understory area.

The home’s smoke alarms also had not been updated in compliance with 2017 laws that applied to any tenancy renewed after January 2022 imposing additional safety measures for alarms.

The homeowner claimed not to have been aware of the legislative change, the court heard.

“[The mother] says that she raised the issue of non-working smoke alarms with the home’s owner, but nothing was done about it,” Leach told the court.

“No witness recalls hearing a smoke alarm sounding at all prior or during the fire.”

MacKenzie has been tasked with investigating seven issues, including whether legally installed fire alarms might have prevented the deaths, and whether the emergency service response to the fire was adequate.

He will also consider whether the presence of any additional emergency service resources located on the island could have prevented the deaths.

Fire investigators have been unable to identify the cause of the blaze, and could not categorically rule out that it was lit deliberately, the court heard.

The inquest has been listed to sit for 10 days in November, to hear from 16 witnesses.

australia.title: Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithms
australia.snippet: Draft legislation enforces digital duty of care including limiting children’s exposure to misogynistic and eating disorder content Austra...
australia.content:
Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.

Users over 16 years of age will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with platforms facing fines of more than A$100m for non-compliance.

Under the plan – dubbed “my feed, my way” – users opting out of the algorithm will see content only from individuals and groups they have actively chosen to follow.

Users would be asked what they want their default feed to be through a pop-up message provided on their platform of choice.

New laws designed to provide a digital duty of care for social media users under 18 will also require services such as online games, apps and AI chatbots to protect children from specific harms.

They will include pornography; content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.

The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to social media companies, with platform operators required to document measures taken to address online harms.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is expected to highlight the plans at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.

“This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control,” he said.

Albanese dismissed concerns of possible retaliation by big tech platforms, and their owners, many of whom have close relationships with the US president, Donald Trump.

The Labor government will require the support of the Greens to advance the laws through parliament. The opposition Liberals and Nationals have flagged opposition, warning the government against efforts to censor the internet.

“Of course there will be opponents, because what this is about is changing the power relationship,” Albanese said.

“We’re taking power from big global tech companies and giving it to ordinary Australians. That is what we are doing. It’s the right thing to do.”

The communications minister, Anika Wells, said tech companies had for too long been allowed to run real-time, unregulated product testing on Australian users.

“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she said. “And it started here in Australia, with the introduction of our world-leading social media minimum age laws.”

The legislation is expected to be introduced to parliament before Christmas, but will likely face a lengthy public inquiry and negotiations.

The Greens communications spokesperson, Sarah Hanson-Young, warned the draft legislation should have a lower threshold for harm, and penalties for platforms should be a percentage of their global revenue.

“Opt out is not acceptable,” she said.

“Opt out is a recipe for big tech to manipulate and to get around it. They’ve got a lot of money, and we know that big tech will be looking for every crack, every possible workaround. So we need to tighten this up and make sure it is watertight.”

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said Labor could not be trusted with “censorship powers”.

“Rather than trying to rig the algorithm, the government should focus on fixing the problems of too high prices, too much tax and too much migration.”

A spokesperson for DIGI, the lobby group representing tech companies including Meta, Snapchat and Google, defended algorithms as helpful to users seeking diverse content.

“We also recognise there is community concern about how these systems work and DIGI welcomes the discussion on the role of recommender systems in online safety,” they said.

“We support an approach that gives people meaningful choice and control over the content they see, while managing safety risks.”

Campaigner Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, called the draft laws a good first step by the government.

“This reform sends the right message to Big Tech,” she said. “You cannot introduce harmful features into our digital lives without asking for our consent first.”

Tom Mooney, campaign director for Democracy Counts, an alliance of organisations concerned about the function of democratic institutions in Australia, said common facts and diversity of opinion was essential.

“Social media is where the majority of Australians get their news, where many people spend hours each day,” he said. “It is common sense to require platforms to give users choice over those experiences.”

Countries including France, Britain and New Zealand are following Australia in implementing social media bans for children, even as expert research showed the systems put in place in Australia in December is only partly effective.

What we learned today, Tuesday 8 September

That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today.

Before we say goodnight, let’s look at what made the top headlines:

  • Former prime minister John Howard has warned political parties against banning migration from certain countries as the debate over Australia’s immigration settings continues.

  • Barnaby Joyce has defended One Nation’s super policy, saying it would have a “minute” impact on inflation. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has savaged the plan, saying it was a threat to the compulsory super rules.

  • The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has announced two key pieces of legislation will be introduced to parliament this week to tackle corruption in the state.

  • Lawyers for an outlawed neo-Nazi political party have argued anti-hate laws passed after the Bondi terror attack rely on the opinion of a politician and are “authoritarian in nature”.

  • Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.

  • Jim Chalmers will release the latest intergenerational report on 21 September, which the treasurer described as “a snapshot of all of the changes we expect to see in our economy and in our society over the next 40 years”.

  • Rising fuel prices, fears of further interest rate hikes and falling house prices have taken household confidence back towards the “deeply pessimistic” levels of last year, according to Westpac’s latest monthly survey.

  • Guardian Australia and the ABC were once again refused entry to a One Nation press conference in Victoria.

  • A dairy company founder and his daughter have been identified as the two people killed in a light plane crash, prompting heartfelt tributes and condolences.

  • About 80 protesters gathered to demand an independent investigation into the death of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.

  • Workers at the Arts Centre Melbourne have voted to go on strike for a full 24 hours this Friday, disrupting a one-night-only performance by US singer Macy Gray and the opening night of an international dance act.

  • Another Australian citizen, who was in Nepal and uncontactable, has today been confirmed safe and well and not requiring consular assistance. There are still 35 Australians missing.

Thanks for sticking around, see you tomorrow morning!

Australian found safe following Nepal-Tibet flood disaster

An Australian citizen, who was in Nepal and uncontactable, has today been confirmed safe and well and not requiring consular assistance.

There are still 35 Australians who remain unaccounted for in the region.

Read more:

Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom accuse One Nation of ‘practising censorship’ after shunning reporters from press conference

Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom have criticised One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, for barring reporters from a press conference.

Reporters from Guardian Australia and the ABC were escorted to the press conference at Crown Melbourne by hotel staff before they were asked which media outlet they were from and told to leave.

AJF’s executive director, Peter Greste, said:

Australia’s strong democracy means journalists have the ability to interrogate politicians on the behalf of the people who hire them – the voters. It isn’t always comfortable, but that freedom is one of the reasons our political system is one of the world’s most stable and effective.

No individual politicians or political party should have the right to choose whether a media outlet can scrutinise them. This is democracy 101, when transparency and accountability are lost, citizens are deprived of their right and ability to know what is going on.

Any politician deciding who gets to scrutinise them is practising censorship, and in a democracy, that’s something we should never accept.

Following the latest updates in the Alan Jones trial?

Nour Haydar and Amanda Meade will be answering reader questions in an upcoming podcast episode of Alan Jones on Trial.

If there’s a piece of evidence, legal process, or courtroom exchange you would like them to explain, submit your question via email to australia.fullstory@theguardian.com.

Arts Centre Melbourne workers call 24-hour strike

Stephanie Convery

Workers at the Arts Centre Melbourne have voted to go on strike for a full 24 hours this Friday, disrupting a one-night-only performance of US singer Macy Gray and the opening night of international dance act, Burn the Floor: Luminous.

Striking workers – including ushers, food and beverage attendants, stage managers, ticketing staff and more – will establish a picket line from 3.30pm and hold a rally from 6pm outside Hamer Hall, where Gray is scheduled to perform, on Friday.

The state government-run Arts Centre is Australia’s largest performing arts venue, employing around 900 workers, some 600 of whom are casuals. Hundreds are expected to join the strike.

The Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA), the Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) Victoria, and the Electrical Trades Union have been bargaining with the Arts Centre on a new enterprise agreement since March.

Pay remains the sticking point. The expired enterprise agreement saw wages increase by 1% every six months, and many of the lowest (Band 1) wages in the expired agreement are now well below the national minimum wage. More than a third of employees are classified as Band 1.

A spokesperson for the Arts Centre said all workers were paid at least the national minimum wage and that they had immediately adjusted the pay of workers whose wages had fallen below national baselines after the Fair Work Commission’s 2026 annual wage review.

The Arts Centre has offered workers a pay rise of 3% annually, the equivalent of the Victorian government wages cap. But workers say they need a 7% annual pay rise to make up for wage stagnation since 2022.

A union petition in support of the workers calling on the state government to increase funding to the arts and arts workers had nearly 3000 signatures at the time of writing.

CPSU Vic Secretary, Jiselle Hanna, said:

The decision to interrupt Macy Gray’s show has not been made lightly – but we are left with no choice until the government funds the Arts Centre properly.

Vicki Ward (Minister for Creative Industries) has the opportunity to sweep in and stop this industrial action by committing to paying workers fairly.

MEAA deputy chief executive, Adam Portelli, said:

Workers are at a point where they simply can’t afford to accept another agreement that leaves them falling behind.

This is about protecting the future of a major cultural institution as much as it is about workers’ pay.

‘They have let down Zomi’: protesters call for justice for slain aid worker

Outside the gates of Israel’s Canberra embassy, a lonely saxophone played as about 80 protesters gathered on Tuesday to demand an independent investigation into the death of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.

Frankcom was killed by the Israel Defense Forces in April 2024 alongside other humanitarians while driving to deliver basic aid to the Gaza Strip.

The findings of an Israeli investigation last month suggested there was no suspicion of criminal misconduct surrounding her death despite a previous finding there had been failures in how the attack was carried out. No charges were laid.

A group, dressed in red to symbolise blood, passed between them a white, tightly bound cloth, designed to look like the dead body of a baby, AAP reports.

Mourning the life of his wife’s oldest friend, Karuna Ratna Bajracharya told the crowd:

I’m losing my faith in humanity when there is no justice.

I can see that when our leaders fail us, when justice fails, when international law fails.

The protesters called for the Israeli ambassador, Hillel Newman, to be expelled from Australia. At the time Newman said he felt deep sorrow for Frankcom’s family but refused to apologise for the strikes on aid vehicles.

Protesters say the response did not go far enough. Bajracharya, a lifelong Labor voter, said he was disheartened by the government’s sustained ties with Israel. He said:

They have let me down dramatically. They have let down Zomi Frankcom.

A letter to the minister in late August, understood to have been written by Australians previously onboard a Gaza-bound Global Sumud Flotilla, demanded an independent investigation into the IDF’s actions.

The group had not yet heard back, Jewish pro-Palestinian activist Anny Mokotow told the crowd. Before reading out the letter, Mokotow said:

We have to fight against this as much as possible. We do it for Zomi Frankcom and those who have died senselessly with her – for their bravery, generosity and selflessness.

Stephanie Convery

Federal eSafety commissioner failed to participate in Victorian inquiry into LGBTQ+ hate crimes, report reveals

Despite the centrality of apps and social media-type platforms to the incidents that triggered the Victorian government inquiry into anti‑LGBTQ+ hate crimes, the federal eSafety commissioner did not participate in it.

Finding 37 of the report said:

The Committee is disappointed that the federal eSafety Commissioner declined to participate in this Inquiry.

The committee found that the community felt social media platforms should take greater responsibility for the “harmful targeting” of LGBTQ+ people on their platforms.

It also recommended the state government advocate to the federal government for “a dedicated inquiry into best practice safety features of dating apps utilised by Australian users”, and to ensure that all apps operated under “an enforceable and strengthened Australian Online Dating Code”.

Grindr and Match Group participated in the inquiry, but other apps did not.

Stephanie Convery

Victorian inquiry into LGBTQ+ hate crimes hands down findings

Hate crimes against the LGBTQ+ community are under-reported, often not recognised as hate crimes by police, and frequently committed by “thrillseekers” enabled by “the relative permissibility of homophobic acts in society”, a Victorian government inquiry has found.

A legislative council inquiry into anti‑LGBTQ+ hate crimes in Victoria handed down its final report to parliament this afternoon. It included 41 findings and 35 recommendations to the state government to strengthen prevention and policing of hate crime related to gender or sexuality, and to fund LGBTQ+ health and community organisations and legal centres to better support victims and the wider community.

The inquiry found that there was significant mistrust of law enforcement among the LGBTQ+ community, which led to under-reporting of crimes against them.

It also found police often did not recognise or record the prejudicial element of the hate crime when it was reported. The committee recommended practical tools be developed to stop hate crime falling through administrative cracks in law enforcement, and an independent evaluation of Victoria police’s LGBTQ+ awareness training.

The inquiry was established after Guardian Australia reported in 2024 on a spate of more than a dozen, separate cases of gay men being allegedly attacked by people they met through dating apps.

Tributes for father and daughter killed in plane crash

A dairy company founder and his daughter have been identified as the two people killed in a light plane crash, prompting heartfelt tributes and condolences, AAP reports.

Ian Campbell, 56, and his daughter Hannah, 23, died on Monday morning when the aircraft crashed south of Brisbane, sparking a large grass fire.

Tributes to the father and daughter highlighted the family’s support for their local community and Campbell’s contributions to the agricultural sector.

The fourth-generation dairy farmer founded the Barambah Organics dairy farming company in Queensland and also ran Manana Pastoral in the Goondiwindi region, producing olive oil, lamb and beef.

Goondiwindi mayor Lawrence Springborg said the family had the support, prayers and goodwill of the community, and the pair would be greatly missed. Campbell founded the Barambah Organics dairy farming company with his wife, Jane.

Springborg told the ABC:

We feel their grief deeply and what makes it also so hard is that the Campbell family were so generous in their support of the local community.

The Campbell family had raised more than $70,000 for the Royal Flying Doctor Service and invested in agriculture, Springborg noted.

National Farmers’ Federation president Hamish McIntyre said the loss of the father and daughter was an “absolutely heartbreaking tragedy”.

Campbell was a highly respected figure in Australian agriculture and a longtime friend, he said.

Hannah was a bright young woman with her whole life in front of her.

McIntyre said his thoughts were with the family, their many friends and everyone touched by “this devastating loss’’.

Guardian Australia and ABC denied access to One Nation press conference

Benita Kolovos

Guardian Australia and the ABC have again been refused entry to a One Nation press conference in Victoria.

One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, is due to address the media over allegations made against him by an ex-partner about alleged drug use.

Reporters from Guardian Australia and the ABC were escorted to the press conference at Crown Melbourne by hotel staff before they were asked which media outlet they were from and told to leave.

Pickering has rejected his ex-partner’s claims as “false”. According to The Australian, he said in a statement:

They are extremely hurtful and I just hope the public can see through them.

Reporters from The Australian, who broke the story, were not barred from attending the press conference.

Krishani Dhanji

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • The opposition started on housing, trying to pressure the government over its building targets, and the impact of its housing tax policies.

  • They then pivoted to the tobacco excise and tried to wedge the government over some comments from NSW Labor premier Chris Minns questioning the current excise level.

  • The health minister, Mark Butler, accused Angus Taylor of playing “follow the leader” with Pauline Hanson – the Coalition has pledged to cut the excise by 80% (a week after One Nation promised a 75% cut).

  • Independent Dai Le asked the government to review her outer western Sydney electorate’s health priority status to bring in more doctors, but Butler said it was “complicated”.

I’ll be honest, it felt like a pretty long and dry question time to me.

And on that note, I’ll leave you with the fabulous Achol Arok for the rest of the afternoon. See you back here bright and early tomorrow!

Two-thirds of households predict another RBA rate hike

Patrick Commins

Rising fuel prices, fears of further interest rate hikes and falling house prices have taken household confidence back towards the “deeply pessimistic” levels of last year, according to Westpac’s latest monthly survey.

Two-thirds of respondents now expect mortgage rates to rise, the survey showed, reflecting a near consensus among economists that the Reserve Bank will hike again this year and potentially as early as later this month.

Matthew Hassan, Westpac’s head of forecasting, said fears of higher rates were weighing particularly heavily on the mood of mortgaged homeowners.

As petrol prices push back towards $2.10 a litre, Hassan said “the mortgage belt is tightening up on spending plans”.

Westpac’s gauge of house price expectations dipped but showed more respondents expected prices to be higher over the next 12 months than lower. A little over 32% expect property values to decline over the coming year, with 20% expecting no change and 42% anticipating an increase (6% weren’t sure).

Westpac also today has joined the other major banks in predicting the RBA will hike again, picking the November meeting as the most likely time.

Luci Ellis, Westpac’s chief economist, said, the main reasons for changing the call “are the growing evidence of a more resilient household sector, and a larger-than-expected impetus from a datacentre focused investment boom”.

While the housing sector is playing out weaker than earlier forecast, the outlook for overall growth is now firmer and the tech sector is adding new cost pressures not evident previously.

Chalmers to release latest intergenerational report with AI a major feature

Patrick Commins

Jim Chalmers will release the latest intergenerational report on 21 September, which the treasurer described as “a snapshot of all of the changes we expect to see in our economy and in our society over the next 40 years”.

The government is required to release an IGR at least every five years under the charter of budget honesty, but can be more frequent (the most recent was in 2023).

In the words of Treasury officials, the reports “examine the long-term sustainability of current policies and how demographic, technological and other structural trends may affect the economy and the budget”.

Artificial intelligence is likely to be a major feature of this year’s report, given its potential to transform the way we work and live over coming years and decades.

That said, Treasury officials have already advised they expect AI will only help productivity growth return to historical levels, rather than unleash a new wave of prosperity.

The IGR will also look at the effects of an ageing population on the economy and the country’s finances. The last IGR highlighted how compulsory super had lightened the burden of paying for aged pensions.

The first IGR was delivered in 2002 under then treasurer Peter Costello, and this year’s report will be the seventh.

After a final dixer to Mark Butler, the PM calls time on QT. Kate Chaney stands up looking annoyed – she was probably due to get the next question.

Liberal MP Garth Hamilton asks Anthony Albanese if he will scrap a $5,000 cap on allied health services for veterans, instead of spending $150m on an “overseas climate talk fest” (the COP climate summit). It’s an issue the opposition pushed heavily last sitting fortnight – and called for the minister responsible to be sacked.

Albanese says the government has increased the fees for allied health workers to stop disincentivising treatment for veterans.

Now the review is after $5,000, that will be more than 12 visits. And then, if further care is required, if there’s a clinical need, then they’ll receive it. Importantly, changes will not impact veterans on the special rate disability pension, on the totally and permanently incapacitated pension, or determined to be catastrophic injured. These changes come into effect on July 27, and the government continues to consult.

Butler refutes claim tobacco policies have ‘led to more Australians smoking illicit cigarettes’

Take three: Liberal MP Mary Aldred, who was on a Coalition-led parliamentary inquiry that recommended cutting the tobacco excise, has a go now to corner the government over the policy.

She again quotes NSW premier Chris Minns warning on the impact of the excise policy, and asks if the health minister will “admit Labor’s failed tobacco policies have led to more Australians smoking illicit cigarettes?”

The health minister, Mark Butler, says he begs to differ and that smoking rates have been going down despite the hiked up excise.

I don’t agree with that. The Institute of Health and Welfare, which has been the statutory authority under governments of both political persuasions for many, many years, says otherwise as well.

I think we should all be glad the authoritative body set up under statute, supported at least until today, by both major political parties, have said that smoking rates over the last three years have declined by about half a million on daily adult smoking rates.

Labor fumes over Coalition question on tobacco excise

Nationals frontbencher Anne Webster asks the assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, why he is “refusing to protect his own constituents” by supporting an excise cut, after a tobacco store in his electorate was firebombed overnight. Mulino was asked about the firebombing in an interview this morning but wouldn’t provide any details on it.

There’s a bunch of back and forth over whether the question is within standing orders or not. Milton Dick calls part of the question a slur, and the government argues that it doesn’t go to Mulino’s portfolio at all.

Webster has another crack and asks why Mulino is “refusing to protect Australians …” which gets some more groans and Dick once again tells Webster to remove that part of the question completely.

Finally we get to the answer.

Mulino defends himself, saying he did answer the question about the firebombing responsibly, because, “what would’ve been irresponsible is for me to speculate on live TV about what actually happened this morning and what might have driven it.”

Can I quote the illicit tobacco and e-cigarette commissioner: ‘Lowering tax on its own is not likely to resolve the criminal side of the market. It does not remove demand, eliminate supply, or the underlying profit opportunities, they, as the organised criminals, can undercut prices no matter where we see the excise.’ We have said repeatedly a responsible approach is to continue our policy on enforcement.

Opposition playing ‘follow the leader’ on tobacco excise, Butler says

Angus Taylor gets on to the wedge train and tries to pressure the government over comments from NSW Labor premier Chris Minns again, this time on the tobacco excise.

This morning Minns (who has publicly questioned the efficacy of the excise remaining high) said: “It’s perversely driving a situation where you’re seeing more people, not less people, smoking because they’ve got access to readily available cheap [black market] cigarettes.

The health minister, Mark Butler, says the government is “not interested in joining the Coalition, in following the leader, that he pathetically appears committed to be playing with the One Nation party”.

We’re not interested in joining the Coalition in a price discounting war with organised crime.

We won’t be joining in a policy plucked out of thin air, with one apparent objective, to go a little bit further than One Nation … And the member for New England [Barnaby Joyce] is pumping his fist. He knows what’s going on here. They know this follow the leader game that he’s playing.

In the middle of his answer, Labor MP Matt Burnell gets kicked out for shouting too much.

australia.title: One Nation’s Warren Pickering admits to illegal drug use and says he is ‘no angel’ in extraordinary press conference
australia.snippet: Victorian One Nation leader says his actions ‘hurt people I loved, and I will live with that forever’ Follow our Australia news live blog...
australia.content:
The Victorian One Nation leader, Warren Pickering, has admitted he “made mistakes” in his 20s, including using ecstasy, methamphetamines and marijuana, losing his licence multiple times for drink driving and hurting people he loved.

But he has denied claims by his ex-partner, published by The Australian, that he smoked ice – also known as crystal meth – in front of children and said he was considering legal action against the publication at a press conference on Tuesday. Guardian Australia and the ABC were barred from attending the press conference.

Accompanied by James Ashby, One Nation’s national director, and his daughter and stepson, Pickering said he was “no angel” as a young man and used illegal drugs in his 20s.

“Never would I have ever said that I was somebody who was a drug addict. I did use them … as a young man and I’m not proud of that,” Pickering said.

He listed ecstasy, methamphetamine, speed and marijuana, but denied using ice or smoking it while his children were home.

“No, I did not,” Pickering said, when asked directly.

Pressed by a reporter about whether he had used ice, Pickering said “ice is not on that list.”

When the reporter said methamphetamines are ice, Pickering replied: “Well, speed”.

“Look, guys, I’m clearly not as familiar with the terms … as you would like me to be,” he said.

“I wasn’t an experienced drug taker.”

Pickering also confirmed he lost his driver’s licence three times for drink driving.

“I believe I lost my licence for drink driving as an 18-year-old, and again as a 20-year-old, and then probably a decade later, I believe they were low-level drink driving,” he said.

Pickering said his actions “hurt people I loved, and I will live with that forever”. But he said he had “changed his life dramatically” for the sake of his daughter and three stepsons, stopped using drugs and joined the Australian Defence Force, which he said gave him a sense of purpose.

“That’s what inspired me to engage in the political sphere to provide service to community in a different way, post-service,” he said.

Ashby also spoke, telling reporters a handwritten note from Pickering published by The Australian, which references “sexual deviance”, was in relation to “behaviour that involved the couple’s open relationship”.

“They opened that relationship to a third person, and at the same time, Mr Pickering was exploring his own sexuality,” Ashby said.

Pickering said he was “working with the lawyers” to get the stories taken down and was receiving advice about possible defamation action.

Reporters from The Australian were able to attend the press conference at Crown Casino. However, reporters from both Guardian Australia and the ABC were asked by Ashby to leave after identifying the media outlet they worked for.

australia.title: Ban on neo-Nazi White Australia party is ‘authoritarian’ and breaches constitution, high court hears
australia.snippet: Lawyers also argue commonwealth does not have the power to ban a political party, as the high court ruled in 1951 over attempt to ban the...
australia.content:
Lawyers for an outlawed neo-Nazi political party have argued anti-hate laws passed after the Bondi terror attack rely on the opinion of a politician and are “authoritarian in nature”.

The White Australia party, formerly known as the National Socialist Network (NSN), was designated as an illegal hate group in May after the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation passed on its recommendation to the home affairs minister, Tony Burke.

The listing means that activities including supporting, funding, training, recruiting and joining the group constitute a criminal offence with a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison.

The far-right nationalist party is challenging the ban at the high court over two days this week, with its lawyers arguing the law breaches the implied freedom of political communication and that handing the decision to Burke breaches the separation of powers.

Lawyers also argued the commonwealth does not have the power to ban political parties, citing a major cold war-era high court ruling in 1951, which overturned a ban on the Communist party of Australia.

If successful, the ruling could wind back the laws that have also banned the Islamist group Hizb ut-Tahrir.

On Tuesday, the group’s barristers, Peter King and Shahed Sharify, argued a total ban on the party was akin to using a “sledgehammer on a nut”.

The arguments centre on proving part 5.3B of the criminal code – which allows the federal police minister to recommend to the attorney general that a group is listed as a prohibited hate group – is invalid.

Sharify argued the law’s breach of implied freedom of political communication was “authoritarian in nature” and suggested it could be used to ban any political party where its members had threatened or engaged in a hate crime with the assistance of the organisation.

The barrister said the banning of hate groups was determined by a politician, based on an opinion with no judicial fairness to appeal that decision.

Sharify said the law’s purposes would be better served by handing that decision to a judge rather than a “busy minister who flicks through a brief and decides in two hours”.

Acting for the government, Brendan Lim, denied the laws could be used for the “illegitimate purpose of quelling political competition”.

“It can’t happen,” he said.

Groups can be listed if it is considered “reasonably necessary to protect the Australian community or part of the Australian community against social, psychological, physical or economic harm”.

Under the rules, Burke must receive advice from the head of Asio recommending that an organisation be considered for listing. The home affairs minister must then receive written agreement from the attorney general and brief the opposition leader.

Unlike the terrorist group listing, a listed hate group cannot make a de-listing application.

The government is also expected to defend the anti-hate laws by arguing the party is not a political party but an arm of White Australia, itself a rebranded version of NSN.

“Forming a political party was a calculated attempt to secure legal protection for members engaging in openly racist and anti-Semitic speech,” the commonwealth said in written submissions.

Members of the White Australia party sat in the front of the courtroom’s public benches, including its leader, Tom Sewell.

The 33-year-old was sentenced in June to a community corrections order – which includes 200 hours of community work – for behaving in an offensive manner in public.

A Melbourne magistrate had found the neo-Nazi leader emulated “Nazi thugs of 1930s Berlin” when he used “appalling racial slurs” during a stunt outside a Chinese consulate.

world.title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia
world.snippet: US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa The scourge of Somali...
world.content:
The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.

Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.

Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.

The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.

However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.

In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.

He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”

According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”

Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.

Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.

Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.

Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.

According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.

Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.

That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.

In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.

During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.

Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.

The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.

Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.

“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.

“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.

“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”

world.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
world.snippet: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive hea...
world.content:
Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.

Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.

This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.

The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.

Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s celsius (high 90s fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

world.title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime
world.snippet: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known...
world.content:
An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.

The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.

The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.

The verdict is subject to appeal.

Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.

Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.

The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.

Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.

According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

world.title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
world.snippet: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland The United Nations has ...
world.content:
The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.

At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.

Togo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of the African Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.

Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.”

The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.

On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies. France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution.

Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.

Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”

He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

world.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border Europe live – latest update...
world.content:
Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.

Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.

Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.

Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.

There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.

“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.

Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa
